power.title: Power Analysis Check
report:
::: {.callout-tip title="Learn More" collapse="true"}

Power analyses need to contain the following information to be interpretable: the type of power analysis, the statistical test, the software used, sample size, critical alpha criterion, power level, effect size, and an effect size metric. In addition, it is recommended to make sure the power analysis is reproducible (by sharing the code, or a screenshot, of the power analysis), and to provide good arguments for why the study was designed to detect an effect of this size.

For an a-priori power analysis, where the sample size is determined, reporting all information would look like:

> An a priori power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that for a Cohen's d = 0.5, an alpha level of 0.05, and a desired power level of 80% required at least 64 participants in each group.

For a sensitivity power analysis, this sentence would look like:

> A sensitivity power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that with 64 participants in each group, and an alpha level of 0.05, a desired power level of 80% was reached for an effect size of d = 0.5.

:::

text.text: This paper introduces the concept of multiple, parallel specifications of hypothesis-testing flexibilities.
Although its ideas are not entirely novel, the conception as a whole has not yet been fully explicated.
It allows researchers other than the study conductors to test a given hypothesis according to their own specifications of how to formulate the hypothesis, collect data, and analyze them.
In practice, Programmatic Registered Reports, which were originally designed for another purpose, already provide an implementation framework requiring only minor additions.
Incorporating a priori specifications by others might necessitate small, feasible extensions to the study design, for example, collecting further outcome measures.

Conceptually, allowing different specifications in hypothesis testing accommodates scientific pluralism while extending the epistemic benefits of preregistration to researchers beyond the study conductors.
Further flexibilities in testing involve data processing and the decision rule for determining whether a hypothesis is corroborated.
Existing approaches, including secondary data analysis, multiverse analysis, and sensitivity analysis, do not address the flexibilities that occur before data processing.
They also have epistemic drawbacks because they rely on post hoc assessments.
The paper discusses the value and scope of the resulting multiple test results, which are conditional on the specifications and their underlying substantive assumptions.
It concludes with a brief discussion of flexibilities in exploratory research.

Flexibilities, also known as 'researchers' degrees of freedom', encompass the entire research process, from a hypothesis's formulation to deciding which results would corroborate the hypothesis and which would not.

Flexibilities are both desired and undesired: desired because they offer adaptability in responding to various demands and uncertainties across different disciplines and particular fields of science; undesired because they can easily give rise to a vast number of results, thereby opening the door to fishing for the desired one (Gelman & Loken, 2013; Hendriks, 2026; Tyner et al., 2026).
text.formatted: Flexibilities are both desired and undesired: desired because they offer adaptability in responding to various demands and uncertainties across different disciplines and particular fields of science; undesired because they can easily give rise to a vast number of results, thereby opening the door to fishing for the desired one <ref type="bibr" target="#b16">(Gelman & Loken, 2013;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b22">Hendriks, 2026;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b59">Tyner et al., 2026)</ref>.

text.text: After reviewing current approaches to disclosing flexibilities in confirmatory research and their limitations, I will introduce the concept of multiple, parallel specifications of flexibilities before data collection.
The concept invites researchers other than those conducting the study to test the hypothesis under different specifications that reflect different underlying substantive assumptions.
A toy example illustrates what this could look like and what can be inferred from the resulting parallel, potentially different, test results.
I outline how the concept can be implemented within the existing framework of Programmatic Registered Reports (PRRs).
The paper ends by showing that these discussions naturally yield implications for the role of exploratory research in this context.
In practice, it is often unclear how several flexibilities in research procedures have been specified in arriving at a published claim that a hypothesis was supported (Scheel, 2022).
text.formatted: In practice, it is often unclear how several flexibilities in research procedures have been specified in arriving at a published claim that a hypothesis was supported <ref type="bibr" target="#b50">(Scheel, 2022)</ref>.

Such weak spots may conceal questionable research practices and may be identified (Höfler et al., 2025).
text.formatted: Such weak spots may conceal questionable research practices and may be identified <ref type="bibr" target="#b27">(Höfler et al., 2025)</ref>.

text.text: The most rigorous way to prevent fishing expeditions when testing a given hypothesis is to disclose the degrees of freedom before the data are collected, or at least before researchers gain access to the data.
This has well-known benefits: 1.
Decisions on the flexibilities are not influenced by what is found in the data (Lakens et al., 2024).
text.formatted: Decisions on the flexibilities are not influenced by what is found in the data <ref type="bibr" target="#b35">(Lakens et al., 2024)</ref>.

text.text: Researchers are held accountable for their predictions (Mayo, 2018) and can later take credit for them (Wagenmakers & Dutilh, 2016).
text.formatted: Researchers are held accountable for their predictions <ref type="bibr" target="#b39">(Mayo, 2018)</ref> and can later take credit for them <ref type="bibr" target="#b61">(Wagenmakers & Dutilh, 2016)</ref>.

text.text: If a prediction turns out to be correct, researchers can point out how it could have turned out otherwise; that is, readers gain an idea of the hypothesis' falsifiability (Höfler et al., 2025; Lakens et al., 2024; Mayo, 2018).

text.text: To ensure that these benefits hold, one needs to verify that flexibilities have actually been disclosed.
Preregistration documents the plan for disclosing the flexibilities, and registered reports promote the actual checking of preregistrations by requesting reviewers to do so (Lakens et al., 2024).

text.text: According to Lakens and DeBruine (2021), rigorous hypothesis testing is guaranteed if all flexibilities in the entire research process are disclosed so that the result is determined after data collection is complete.

text.text: 'Result' means that the hypothesis is either corroborated or not.

A binary test result has been argued to be warranted because the decisions informed by statistical tests (e.g., on theory and intervention) are binary in nature (Lakens et al., 2018; Höfler et al., to appear).

Novel approach: Parallel Specifications of Flexibilities
Concept I formulate a concept that overcomes the pitfalls of post hoc assessment and considers much fewer variants than commonly examined in multiverse analysis.

It grounds on familiar ideas, but has not been fully explicated as a conception guided by the principle of extending the epistemic benefits of preregistering flexibilities before access to data to researchers other than the study conductors.

This extends the idea of parallel specifications of an analysis within a given dataset, as exemplified by 'Many Analysts, One Dataset' (Silberzahn et al., 2018) and 'Synchronous Robustness Reports' (Bartoš et al., 2025), to the entire research process.

text.text: In my concept, the study conductors develop a study design and specify which flexibilities it accommodates and the extent to which each can be varied within a study's feasibility limits.
The range of possible variations is determined at this stage.
For example, the study conductors may plan an experiment using a particular paradigm while allowing for the addition of another outcome measure (e.g., a questionnaire score).
In contrast, including a different method (e.g., eye tracking) will commonly not be practicable within the study's budget.
Such a substantial extension would instead require additional funding for a multimethod study (Campbell & Fiske, 1959) at the outset.

text.text: Specifications may also vary in the exact formulation of the hypothesis, as long as the resulting variants can be tested within the same basic study design.
Importantly, the range of possibilities is determined primarily by practical constraints, rather than by whether a variation is considered to alter the hypothesis substantively.
For instance, replacing an outcome measure with another may be feasible but might genuinely change the hypothesis.
Conversely, a modification in the sampled population may be considered a variation of the same hypothesis, but may not be feasible.
After the study conductors have completed their study protocol, a preregistration template is prepared.
This template defines the range within which these flexibilities can be specified differently.
The study plan is then distributed, and other researchers are invited to contribute alternative specifications and their theoretical justifications as a basis for testing the hypothesis.

text.text: In addition to the epistemic benefits, the suggested concept reduces costs in comparison to the common approach.
In particular, the comparison is between: 1.
Many studies: As is common, a hypothesis is tested across different studies (samples), each with a different specification; and 2.
One study: The same study tests the hypothesis under the different specifications.
In the many-studies approach, each set of specifications of the research process necessitates an individual study involving a new sample, resulting in a total of S sets.
If the expenses (money, personnel, recruitment) of a study roughly equal c (assuming similar designs, as in the one-study concept), the total cost of all studies is on the order of S × c.
The actual total costs are expected to be somewhat larger than S × c if multiple specifications require minor extensions to the study design.
I propose a common review process-albeit a more extensive one-for stages 1 and 2 of a PRR.

Having the same reviewers assess the stage 1 proposal and the different variants in stage 2 would increase consistency and create synergies, as reviewers could build on their familiarity with the study rather than independently familiarizing themselves with it.
This approach would reduce the overall reviewing workload for the scientific community.
Cost considerations should also take into account how statistical errors differ between the two approaches.

text.text: This paper has elaborated on the concept of multiple, parallel specifications of research flexibilities, initially set up by the conductors of a study and then opened to others for alternative specifications.
The concept makes use of an existing tool (PRRs), which was designed for another purpose and therefore lacks a detailed conceptual foundation for its application and modification in this context.
This paper has sought to fill this gap, whereas existing approaches to hypothesis testing by others incorporate multiple specifications only from data processing onward.
The concept combines desirable pluralism through allowing flexibilities with the epistemic advantages of disclosing them before accessing the data.
It invites multiple test results, each conditional on a set of specifications and their substantive justifications.
Importantly, the epistemic advantages of these conditional test results apply only to the researchers who actually chose the relevant specifications a priori.
For others, namely researchers who read the results in a paper, these advantages apply only if they, too, would have chosen the same specifications beforehand-a condition that cannot be verified.
It might also be tempting for recipients to aim for a majority vote in the research community on which of the tested specification sets appears most plausible.
This can be misleading because such a vote would constitute a post hoc assessment made with knowledge of the results and might thus be affected by interests in arriving at one result over another.

However, awareness of this issue and discussions about the investigated specification variants might motivate researchers either to participate in future studies involving parallel specifications of flexibilities or to engage in consensus initiatives to reduce flexibilities in the first place.

Another epistemic question should be investigated once parallel preregistrations are established to test the same hypothesis: is such external testing of a hypothesis less susceptible to investigator bias than the common approach of testing the hypothesis in one's own study?

This advantage, if it exists, might be limited insofar as investigator bias is already inherent in the study design selected by the researcher and cannot be addressed through what can be specified in the preregistration template.
Minimizing such risks through detailed study plans and preregistration templates is a key purpose of the review process, and reviewers should be instructed accordingly.
Many practical issues that are outside the scope of this conceptual paper remain to be tested and investigated.
These mainly involve details of implementation in PRRs.
Nevertheless, some general principles can be outlined from the outset: The distribution of an accepted Stage 1 PRR protocol should follow the principles of visibility and inclusivity.
Thus, the 'crowdsourcing' (Silberzahn et al., 2018) of alternative specifications for testing the planned study should provide as many researchers as possible with the opportunity to participate.

Once its idea reaches the scientific community, it may encourage researchers to participate.
This would reduce the overall workload for the scientific community by rendering multiple separate studies to test the same hypothesis less necessary.
Researchers may also be prompted to initiate such studies themselves and to contribute to their refinement and implementation.

In addition to the usual review in (P)RRs, reviewers check that the ranges are large enough to cover what others might justifiably do differently.
If the conductors do not run the alternative tests themselves, the protocol must include everything others need to run them, but not the data.
This may include the syntax reflecting the conductors' specifications, which enables others to prepare their alternative scripts for preregistration.
The study conductors obtain in-principle acceptance for a protocol with their own specification set and the range of feasible modifications.
The Stage 1 protocol is made public.
It includes a deadline for submitting alternative preregistrations (see Step 4).
Other researchers complete the preregistration template with their specifications and justifications, and submit their alternative preregistrations to the editor.
If necessary, the conductors amend the data collection part of the accepted Stage 1 protocol to accommodate the alternative specifications.

The editor or a small reviewer panel checks (a) whether this amendment includes what is necessary to accommodate the alternative specifications and (b) whether the justifications provided in these other preregistrations state the substantive assumptions explicitly and whether the proposed specifications are consistent with those assumptions.
Infeasible proposals are rejected, and authors of proposals with insufficient justification may be asked to revise them.
Once these checks are passed, the study conductors collect the data.
The data are processed and analyzed separately according to each preregistered plan.
Either all analyses are run by the study conductors, or the other researchers run their variants themselves.
The important point is that compliance with the preregistered plans can be verified.
The Stage 2 report of the study conductors can be submitted.

Reviewers make the same checks as in common RRs (the introduction remained unchanged, the hypothesis was tested as preregistered, all deviations are reported and justified, and the conclusions are justified by the results).
In addition, they check that the report states that parallel specification sets exist and refers to the anticipated Stage 2 reports of the other researchers.
